ESR1 mutations and MAPK pathway alterations are significantly mutually exclusive in post-hormonal therapy HR+/HER2- tumors (Fisher's exact test: OR = 0.588, 95% CI [0.387, 0.893], p = 0.012).

In a cohort of 705 post-hormonal therapy HR+/HER2- MSK-IMPACT samples:
- 131 samples (18.6%) harbored ESR1 functional mutations (predominantly D538G, Y537S/C/N, E380Q)
- 261 samples (37.0%) had MAPK pathway alterations (mutations or copy-number changes in BRAF, KRAS, NRAS, NF1, EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, FGFR1/2/4, MAP2K1/2, MAPK1/3, and others)
- Only 36 samples (5.1%) carried both, while 225 had MAPK alterations alone and 95 had ESR1 mutations alone

The mutual exclusivity is strongest at the individual gene level for NF1 (OR = 0.207, p = 0.013) and ERBB2 (OR = 0.109, p = 0.005), while the core RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade alone does not reach significance (p = 0.461). The broader MAPK pathway definition — dominated by FGFR1 amplification (17% of samples) and ERBB2 alterations — drives the pathway-level signal.

Biologically, this mutual exclusivity supports the model that ESR1 gain-of-function mutations (constitutive ER signaling) and MAPK pathway activation (growth factor receptor-driven proliferation) represent alternative, non-redundant genomic mechanisms of endocrine resistance. Tumors that acquire ESR1 LBD mutations achieve ER signaling independence, reducing selective pressure for concurrent MAPK activation. The 27.5% overlap (36/131 ESR1-mutated samples that also have MAPK alterations) represents tumors with dual resistance mechanisms that may require combination therapeutic strategies.
